first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent it, so I read it properly. The opening is calm and sensible, and 'For Australian couples, it also covers safety levels, embassies and carrying the customs home' told me there would be a practical part at the end. I read it top to bottom, though I'll admit the middle got heavy going.

journey.quote: Baltic wedding traditions are usually served up as one list, as if Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius shared a single rulebook. They don't.
journey.reaction: Good. I'd hate to turn up and get the wrong country's customs. Treating each one properly feels respectful.

journey.quote: Smartraveller rates all three countries "Exercise normal safety precautions" overall as at November 2026, and the Australian embassies covering them sit in Stockholm (Estonia and Latvia) and Warsaw (Lithuania).
journey.reaction: Reassuring on safety, and dated, which I like. But Stockholm and Warsaw? That's a long way off if one of the older relatives ends up in hospital.

journey.quote: Treat it as a fixed midnight moment in the run sheet, and ask early whether a folklore group can perform.
journey.reaction: Practical. Though midnight is late for my mother. Worth knowing so we can plan for the older ones to rest beforehand.

journey.quote: Only after the sužadėtuvės, the betrothal rites, which carried legal weight, was the wedding agreed.
journey.reaction: Interesting history, but by this point there are a lot of foreign words in a row and I was skimming. Nothing wrong with it, it's just more than I need to make a decision.

journey.section: 8. Gates and obstacles on the way (Lithuania)
journey.quote: Build slack into your transfer times, and give the best man something to hand over at each gate.
journey.reaction: This is the kind of line I like, telling you what to actually do. More of these, please.

journey.quote: Treat Kihnu as a living community to learn from, with local permission, rather than a backdrop.
For a Latvian wedding, look at Riga and other places well away from that border area.
journey.reaction: Thank you. Instead of just giving me the warning, it tells me where is fine. That settles my nerves.

journey.section: Paperwork and which embassy to ask
journey.quote: DFAT can't advise on another country's legal process, so the first question goes to the local registry or the country's embassy in Australia: is a CNI needed, must it be issued locally, and does it need an apostille?
journey.reaction: Clear about who to ask. I'll forward that to my husband, he'll want to ring them himself.

journey.section: Paperwork and which embassy to ask
journey.quote: The consulates in Tallinn and Riga offer limited help, and the honorary consulate in Vilnius does no notarial acts.
journey.reaction: Honest, but it rather confirms that if something goes wrong over there, help is thin on the ground. So who is our person on the spot?

journey.section: Getting married in Latvia, Lithuania or Estonia as an Australian
journey.quote: Weddings in Latvia, Lithuania or Estonia are possible for Australians, but each country runs its own process. All of this is as at November 2026.
journey.reaction: Fine, but there's nothing in this whole section about getting elderly guests there comfortably. Long flights, transfers, cobbled old towns with a walking frame, travel insurance. That's what keeps me up at night.

journey.quote: You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law; Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm.
journey.reaction: Good that they don't pretend to be lawyers. I want it legal at home with no fuss.

journey.section: Bringing Baltic customs to a wedding at home
journey.quote: One person is your single point of contact, and the fee and inclusions are agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: This is the sentence I was waiting for. One person, everything in writing. It doesn't tell me who, or whether deposits paid overseas are safe, but it's the right start.

unanswered_questions: If we pay deposits to venues or suppliers in the Baltics, is that money protected, and who is responsible if a supplier lets us down?
Are contracts with local suppliers in English, and are quotes in Australian dollars?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong at 2am Riga time? Is there anyone on the ground, given the embassies are in Stockholm and Warsaw?
Can older guests with limited mobility manage the cobbled old towns, churches and venues, and who arranges airport transfers?
What travel insurance should elderly guests have for this trip?
Who is the Wedded Advisor, and can I speak to them on the phone before anything is booked?
would_share_with: My husband, with the safety and embassy sections marked
My daughter, to say this is sensible, let's ring them

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like help shaping it, in Riga, Vilnius, Tallinn or at home, a conversation with a Wedded Advisor is a calm place to start.
cta_reaction.why: 'A conversation' and 'calm' are the right words for me, and the fee in writing reassures me. I'd click if I knew it meant a phone call with a real person rather than a long form, and had some idea how overseas deposits are handled.

top_3_changes: Add a short paragraph for older or less mobile guests: long-haul flights, transfers, cobbled old towns, travel insurance, framed as questions to ask rather than invented details.
Next to the Wedded Advisor line, say plainly what happens after you click (a phone call with a named person) and who helps on the ground, since the embassies are far away.
Ease the dense Lithuanian section a little, for example one plain-English line of 'what this means for your day' per custom, like the excellent gates tip.

Stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent, practical, reads top to bottom)
